Short answer: Yes, you can build this.
Real answer (no sugarcoating): It’s doable, but only if you accept some hard macOS + app-level limitations. Grammarly didn’t get magical access—Apple just gives some hooks, not god-mode.

I’ll break it down cleanly.

What you want (restated clearly)
You want a macOS app that:

Sees text typed anywhere (browser, Cursor, VS Code, WhatsApp Web, Notion, etc.)

Can edit/replace that text (like Grammarly)

Automatically saves sent text / prompts as long-term memory

Surfaces relevant past memory anywhere (Cursor, chat apps, text fields)

All of this happens at the application layer, not via MCPs or per-app APIs

This is basically:

Grammarly + Supermemory + system-wide memory injection

Can macOS technically allow this?
✅ YES — via Accessibility + Input Monitoring
But with important constraints.

macOS gives you 3 critical powers:

1. Reading text from ANY app (Grammarly-style)
How Grammarly actually works
They do NOT read app internals. They use:

🔑 macOS Accessibility API (AXUIElement)
You can:

Detect focused text fields

Read:

Current text

Cursor position

Selected text

Observe:

Text changes

Focus changes

App switches

📌 This works in:

Browsers

Cursor / VS Code

Slack

Notion

WhatsApp

Almost everything that uses standard text inputs

⚠️ Exceptions:

Some custom-rendered apps

Games

Secure fields (passwords)

➡️ This is exactly how Grammarly does it

2. Editing / replacing text system-wide
Also YES.

You can:

Programmatically:

Replace selected text

Insert suggestions

Modify content inline

Methods:

AXUIElementSetAttributeValue

Synthetic keystrokes (fallback)

This gives you:

Inline rewrite

Auto-corrections

“Accept suggestion” behavior

3. Saving everything as memory (Supermemory-style)
This is the easy part.

Flow:
User types / sends message
↓
Accessibility detects text submission (Enter / Send / blur)
↓
You capture final text
↓
Embed + store locally (or encrypted cloud)
↓
Tag with:
  - App
  - Context
  - Timestamp
  - Language
  - Topic
You are not violating macOS rules here if:

You ask permission clearly

Store locally by default

Encrypt memory

4. Retrieving memory ANYWHERE (Cursor, browser, etc.)
This is the tricky-but-possible part.

How you do it:
Option A — Inline ghost suggestions (Grammarly-style)
When user types:

Detect intent

Search memory

Show floating suggestion bubble

User clicks → inserts memory

Option B — Global shortcut (🔥 best UX)
Cmd + Shift + M

Overlay opens

Shows:

Relevant past prompts

Notes

Contextual memory

Click → injects text at cursor

Option C — Passive assist
While typing:

You detect similarity

Subtle hint:
“You wrote something similar before”

5. “Anywhere on Cursor or anywhere” — reality check
❌ You CANNOT:
Inject code directly into Cursor’s internal AI context

Modify Cursor’s LLM behavior internally

Force Cursor to “see” your memory natively

✅ BUT you CAN:
Insert memory into the editor

Paste memory before prompts

Act as a co-pilot layer above Cursor

So practically:

Your app becomes the memory brain, Cursor becomes the executor

This is totally fine and honestly how most people will use it.

6. Architecture (clean & real)
macOS App (Swift / SwiftUI)
Accessibility listener

Text capture

Overlay UI

Permissions manager

Memory Engine (local-first)
SQLite / DuckDB

Vector DB (FAISS / LanceDB)

Encrypted at rest

AI Layer
Local embeddings (recommended)

Optional cloud LLM

Context ranking

Injection Layer
Accessibility write-back

Keystroke fallback

Clipboard-safe paste

7. Permissions you MUST ask for (non-negotiable)
macOS will require:

✅ Accessibility

✅ Input Monitoring

⚠️ Screen Recording (optional, avoid if possible)

Grammarly asks the same.

If users trust Grammarly, they’ll trust this if you’re transparent.

8. Is this allowed by Apple?
Yes IF:

You don’t keylog passwords

You explain what you capture

You allow pause / private mode

You don’t secretly exfiltrate data

Grammarly, Raycast, Alfred all do similar things.

9. Hard truths (important)
❌ This is NOT a weekend project
Expect:

2–3 weeks just to get Accessibility right

Tons of edge cases

Per-app quirks

❌ Perfect coverage is impossible
But 90% coverage = totally achievable.

✅ This is actually a VERY strong product idea
Especially for:

Developers

Writers

Power users

Students (you 👀)

Thought for 12s
Yep — v1 (capture + save text you “send” anywhere) is very buildable on macOS with Accessibility + (optionally) Input Monitoring and a local DB.

Below is (1) how v1 should work, and (2) a copy-paste Cursor prompt that tells Cursor exactly what to build.

How v1 works (macOS-first, app-layer)
Core idea
Run a menu bar app that watches the currently focused text input via the macOS Accessibility API and saves a “finalized message” when you detect “send”.

What you can reliably use
Accessibility (AXUIElement) to read focused text fields and their content/selection. Apple documents focused-element change notifications like kAXFocusedUIElementChangedNotification. 

AXObserverCreate to subscribe to accessibility notifications from apps (focus/value changes). 

Optional: Input Monitoring (or event taps / global monitors) to detect Enter / Cmd+Enter and treat that as “send”. Apple explicitly controls this permission. 

“Send” detection (practical approach)
In v1, don’t try to be perfect. Use a simple heuristic:

Save the current text when any of these happen:

User presses Enter (and/or Cmd+Enter) while focus is in an editable field (requires Input Monitoring or event tap). 

Focus leaves the text field right after a change (AX focus change notification + last edit time) 

Frontmost app changes (AX application activated + focus changes) 

This catches: ChatGPT web, WhatsApp Web, Slack, Cursor editor prompts, Notion comments, etc. It won’t be 100% universal, but it’s very strong for v1.

Local DB
Use SQLite (simple, fast, local-first). Save:

text

app_bundle_id

window_title (if you can read it)

timestamp

source (“enter_key”, “focus_lost”, etc.)

optional: hash to dedupe

Copy-paste Cursor prompt (build v1)
Paste this into Cursor (as-is):

You are a senior macOS engineer. Build a macOS menubar app (Swift + SwiftUI) called “MemoryTap” that captures and stores text the user “sends” from ANY app, locally.

GOAL (V1):
- Run as a menu bar app (no dock icon preferred).
- With user permission, detect the focused editable text field system-wide using macOS Accessibility APIs (AXUIElement).
- Read the current text of the focused field (kAXValueAttribute where available).
- Detect “send” events using a best-effort heuristic:
  A) primary: when the user presses Enter or Cmd+Enter while a text field is focused (requires Input Monitoring permission; use CGEventTapCreate if needed; fallback to NSEvent addGlobalMonitorForEventsMatchingMask).
  B) secondary: if focused element changes away from an editable field shortly after text changed, treat that as finalize/send.
- On “send”, save the finalized text to a local SQLite database.
- Provide a simple UI:
  - Menu bar icon with dropdown:
    - “Start Capturing” / “Pause Capturing”
    - “Open Memory” (shows a basic list of captured items with search)
    - “Privacy Mode” toggle (when ON, do not capture anything; show a clear indicator)
    - “Clear All”
  - A main window listing memories (date, app name, first line), click to view full text, copy button.

NON-GOALS (V1):
- No AI embeddings, no cloud sync, no “insert back” into fields.
- No per-app APIs (no Slack API, no browser extensions, no Cursor plugins).
- Just capture + save locally.

TECH REQUIREMENTS:
1) Permissions & onboarding
- On first launch, show an onboarding screen explaining required permissions:
  - Accessibility permission (to read focused text fields and receive notifications).
  - Input Monitoring permission if using global key detection.
- Provide buttons that deep-link the user to the correct macOS Privacy & Security settings pages where possible, and clear instructions if deep-linking isn’t possible.
- Implement permission checks:
  - Accessibility: AXIsProcessTrustedWithOptions.
  - Input Monitoring: detect whether event tap/monitor works; show instructions if denied.

2) Accessibility layer
- Create a System-wide accessibility element: AXUIElementCreateSystemWide().
- Read:
  - kAXFocusedApplicationAttribute
  - kAXFocusedUIElementAttribute
- For the focused UI element:
  - confirm it’s editable (check role/subrole/AXEditable or supported attributes).
  - attempt to read kAXValueAttribute as String.
- Create an AXObserver for the focused application PID using AXObserverCreate.
- Subscribe to:
  - kAXFocusedUIElementChangedNotification
  - kAXValueChangedNotification (when available)
  - any other relevant text-change notifications exposed by AX.
- Maintain a state machine:
  - currentFocusedElementID (hash/identity)
  - lastKnownText
  - lastEditTimestamp
  - captureEnabled, privacyMode
- When text changes: update lastKnownText and lastEditTimestamp.
- When focus changes: if lastEditTimestamp is recent and lastKnownText is non-empty and differs from previous saved snapshot, finalize/save.

3) Key detection layer (best effort)
- Implement a global key listener:
  - Preferred: CGEventTapCreate at a safe tap point (listen-only).
  - Capture Return/Enter key presses and modifier flags.
- When Enter/Cmd+Enter occurs and focused element is editable:
  - Grab text from focused element immediately (or after a tiny delay on main queue) and save.
- If permissions prevent key detection, rely only on focus/value-change heuristic and show a warning in UI.

4) Local storage (SQLite)
- Implement a lightweight SQLite layer (no heavy ORM).
- Schema:
  table memories(
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    created_at INTEGER,
    app_bundle_id TEXT,
    app_name TEXT,
    window_title TEXT,
    source TEXT,
    text TEXT,
    text_hash TEXT
  )
- Dedupe:
  - compute text_hash (e.g. SHA256 of trimmed text).
  - avoid saving if same hash saved within last 10 seconds from same app.
- Provide CRUD:
  - insertMemory
  - listMemories(paged, search)
  - deleteMemory(id)
  - clearAll

5) UI
- SwiftUI for:
  - Menu bar popover controls
  - Main window list + detail view
- Show capturing status (ON/OFF) and Privacy Mode clearly.

DELIVERABLES:
- Provide a complete Xcode project structure:
  - App entry
  - Permissions manager
  - Accessibility watcher service
  - Key listener service
  - SQLite storage
  - SwiftUI views
- The code must compile.
- Include comments explaining key parts and known limitations (e.g., secure fields cannot be read; some apps may not expose AXValue).
- Include a short README inside the repo describing how to run, grant permissions, and troubleshoot.

IMPORTANT LIMITATIONS TO HANDLE GRACEFULLY:
- Some focused elements return AXError.noValue; do not crash—fallback and keep running.
- Do not capture password/secure fields (detect role/subrole/secure input where possible; otherwise maintain a denylist of common secure roles and skip).
- Provide a “Pause” toggle and “Privacy Mode” toggle. Privacy Mode must override everything.

Now implement this in Swift + SwiftUI with clean modular code.
Why this is the “right” v1
No AI = you’re shipping faster.

Uses the same foundation Grammarly-style tools use: AX focus + value change + observer. 

For detecting “send”, using key detection requires OS permission (Input Monitoring / event taps). Apple explicitly gates this.

Got it. Below is clean, structured, Cursor-ready content exactly how you asked:

1. Context — what we ultimately want to build (best version)
We want to build a macOS system-level memory assistant that works like Grammarly in reach, but like Supermemory in purpose. It should run in the background and understand everything the user types or sends anywhere on their Mac—chat messages, AI prompts, emails, notes, code comments, etc. The app should automatically capture these finalized texts as personal memory, store them locally first, and later surface relevant past memory anywhere the user is typing, regardless of app (Cursor, browser, Slack, Notion, WhatsApp, etc.). This memory system should live at the application layer, not via per-app APIs, MCPs, or plugins, so it works universally with a consistent UI and UX. Over time, it becomes an OS-level “external brain” for the user, independent of any single editor, AI tool, or platform.

2. What we are building right now (V1 — scoped and realistic)
Version 1 is intentionally simple.
We are only building the foundation:

A macOS menu bar app

That can detect and read text the user sends anywhere

And save that text locally as memory

No AI.
No embeddings.
No inserting text back.
No Cursor integration yet.

V1 only answers one question perfectly:

“Can we reliably capture and store the exact text a user sends from any app on macOS?”

If this works well, everything else builds on top of it.

3. Cursor prompt — how to build V1 (copy-paste as is)
You are a senior macOS engineer. Build a macOS menu bar application called “MemoryTap” using Swift + SwiftUI.

====================================
GOAL (VERSION 1)
====================================

Create a macOS system-level app that captures and stores text that a user “sends” or finalizes from ANY application (browser, Cursor, VS Code, Slack, WhatsApp Web, Notion, etc.), using macOS Accessibility APIs — NOT per-app APIs, browser extensions, plugins, MCPs, or cloud hooks.

This app runs in the background and saves captured text locally in a SQLite database.

====================================
CORE FUNCTIONALITY
====================================

1. App Type
- Menu bar app (status bar icon).
- No dock icon preferred.
- Runs continuously once launched.

2. Permissions (mandatory)
- Accessibility permission:
  - To detect focused UI elements
  - To read text from editable fields
- Input Monitoring permission (best effort):
  - To detect Enter / Cmd+Enter key presses
- Implement a clear onboarding screen that:
  - Explains WHY permissions are needed
  - Shows current permission status
  - Guides the user to System Settings if missing

3. Text Detection (Accessibility Layer)
- Use AXUIElementCreateSystemWide()
- Continuously track:
  - Focused application
  - Focused UI element
- For the focused UI element:
  - Verify it is editable (role, subrole, AXEditable, etc.)
  - Attempt to read text using kAXValueAttribute
- Subscribe to accessibility notifications using AXObserver:
  - kAXFocusedUIElementChangedNotification
  - kAXValueChangedNotification (when supported)
- Maintain internal state:
  - current focused element reference
  - last known text
  - last edit timestamp
  - last saved text hash

4. Detecting “Send” (Heuristic-based)
Treat text as “finalized/sent” when ANY of the following occur:

A) Primary method (if Input Monitoring is granted):
- Detect Enter or Cmd+Enter key press globally
- If focused element is editable:
  - Fetch its text immediately (or with a short async delay)
  - Save it as a memory entry

B) Secondary method (Accessibility-only fallback):
- If focused UI element changes away from an editable field
- AND text was edited recently (e.g. within last 2–5 seconds)
- AND text is non-empty and different from last saved snapshot
- Then treat the last known text as finalized and save it

C) App switch heuristic:
- If frontmost application changes shortly after text editing
- Capture last edited text before focus loss

This does not need to be perfect — it needs to be robust for common apps.

5. What NOT to capture
- Secure or password fields
- Detect common secure roles/subroles and skip
- If uncertain, err on the side of NOT capturing

6. Local Storage (SQLite)
Implement a lightweight SQLite storage layer.

Schema:

table memories (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  created_at INTEGER,
  app_bundle_id TEXT,
  app_name TEXT,
  window_title TEXT,
  source TEXT,           -- "enter_key", "focus_lost", "app_switch"
  text TEXT,
  text_hash TEXT
)

- Generate text_hash using SHA256 of trimmed text
- Deduplicate:
  - Do not save if same hash was saved from same app within last 10 seconds

7. Menu Bar UI
Menu bar icon dropdown should include:
- Capture ON / OFF toggle
- Privacy Mode toggle (when ON, absolutely nothing is captured)
- “Open Memory” button
- “Clear All Memories”
- Status indicator showing:
  - Capturing active
  - Privacy mode active

8. Main Window UI
SwiftUI window that:
- Lists saved memories (latest first)
- Shows:
  - App name
  - Timestamp
  - First line / preview of text
- Click to view full text
- Copy button
- Delete individual entry

====================================
ARCHITECTURE REQUIREMENTS
====================================

- Modular design:
  - PermissionsManager
  - AccessibilityWatcher
  - KeyEventListener
  - CaptureCoordinator (decides when to save)
  - MemoryStore (SQLite)
- App must never crash due to AX errors
- Handle AXError.noValue and unsupported attributes gracefully
- Clearly comment known limitations:
  - Some apps do not expose text
  - Secure fields are ignored
  - Some custom editors may not work

====================================
NON-GOALS (STRICT)
====================================

- No AI
- No embeddings
- No cloud sync
- No inserting text back into fields
- No Cursor plugins
- No browser extensions

====================================
DELIVERABLES
====================================

- Complete Swift + SwiftUI project structure
- Code that compiles in Xcode
- Inline comments explaining key macOS behaviors
- Short README explaining:
  - How to run
  - How to grant permissions
  - Known limitations

Build this cleanly, safely, and pragmatically.

What you’re building here is not trivial, but it’s also not fantasy. Grammarly, Raycast, Alfred, and system automation tools prove this layer is real. If V1 works, you’ll have something very few people actually understand how to build.

Good catch — this is an important distinction.
Let me clarify cleanly and honestly, no fluff.

What is a menu bar app on macOS?
A menu bar app is still a real macOS app.
It’s not a widget, not a service, not a background script.

It just means:

It lives in the top-right menu bar (near Wi-Fi, battery, clock)

It doesn’t show a dock icon by default

It can still:

Open full windows

Have settings

Have a database

Run background logic

Ask for permissions

Do everything a normal app can do

Examples you already use:
Grammarly

Raycast

Alfred

Dropbox

Magnet

Rectangle

All of these are actual macOS apps.

Why apps like Grammarly use the menu bar model
Because your app:

Needs to be always running

Needs system-level access

Should be reachable from anywhere

Should not clutter the Dock

If it were a normal Dock-only app:

Users would forget it’s running

It’s harder to show status (paused / privacy mode)

Worse UX for something that’s “ambient”

Can we still have a “proper app window”?
Yes. 100%.

A menu bar app can:

Open a full window

Have:

Memory list

Search

Settings

Debug panel

Behave exactly like a normal app when opened

Think of it like this:

Menu bar = launcher + status
Main window = real app

Two valid designs (pick one)
Option A — Menu bar–first (recommended for this idea)
App launches → menu bar icon appears

Background capture starts

Clicking icon → dropdown

“Open Memory” → opens full window

This is how Grammarly, Raycast, Alfred work.

Option B — Dock app + menu bar (also possible)
App appears in Dock

ALSO adds a menu bar item

Slightly more clutter, but familiar

You can even switch later.

Why I strongly recommend menu bar for your app
Because what you’re building is:

System-wide

Passive

Always-on

Contextual

This is exactly what menu bar apps are for on macOS.

Apple UX-wise:

This is the “correct” pattern

Reviewers expect it

Users trust it

Important clarification (this might surprise you)
A menu bar app is NOT:

Less powerful

Less “real”

Harder to build

It’s literally:

NSStatusBar.system.statusItem(...)
Everything else is the same.

Final recommendation (no sugarcoating)
👉 Build it as a menu bar app that opens a full app window.

That gives you:

Best UX

Best trust

Best alignment with Grammarly / Raycast

Zero technical downside

we need a button that appears when input is selected but where should be its placement thats the question?

see current version, 

//
//  MemoryOverlayManager.swift
//  Cortex
//
//  Manages the floating \"memory\" button overlay and search+insert flow.
//

import Foundation
import AppKit
import SwiftUI

@MainActor
final class MemoryOverlayManager {
    
    private let contextDetector: ContextDetector
    private let searchService: MemorySearchService
    private let insertService: MemoryInsertService
    
    private var window: NSWindow?
    private var isVisible: Bool = false
    
    init(contextDetector: ContextDetector,
         searchService: MemorySearchService,
         insertService: MemoryInsertService) {
        self.contextDetector = contextDetector
        self.searchService = searchService
        self.insertService = insertService
    }
    
    /// Show or update the overlay near the current context, if any.
    func updateOverlayVisibility() {
        guard AppState.shared.captureEnabled,
              !AppState.shared.privacyModeEnabled else {
            hideOverlay()
            return
        }
        
        guard let context = contextDetector.currentContext(),
              !context.text.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines).isEmpty else {
            hideOverlay()
            return
        }
        
        showOverlay(with: context)
        triggerBackgroundSearch(for: context.text)
    }
    
    private func showOverlay(with context: ContextDetector.Context?) {
        // Button size we expect for the overlay window
        let buttonSize = CGSize(width: 32, height: 32)
        let margin: CGFloat = 6
        
        let position: CGPoint
        let primaryScreenHeight = NSScreen.screens.first?.frame.height ?? NSScreen.main?.frame.height ?? 1080
        
        if let context = context {
            // Priority 1: Cursor Frame (Position ABOVE cursor)
            // Note: Cursor width can be 0 (just a line), so we only check height
            if let cursorFrame = context.cursorFrame, cursorFrame.height > 0 {
                // Convert AX cursor frame (Top-Left) to Cocoa frame (Bottom-Left)
                let cocoaCursorY = primaryScreenHeight - cursorFrame.maxY
                let cocoaCursorFrame = CGRect(x: cursorFrame.origin.x, y: cocoaCursorY, width: cursorFrame.width, height: cursorFrame.height)
                
                // Find screen for cursor
                let screen = NSScreen.screens.first { screen in
                    screen.frame.intersects(cocoaCursorFrame)
                } ?? NSScreen.main
                let screenFrame = screen?.frame ?? CGRect(x: 0, y: 0, width: 800, height: 600)
                
                // Position: Centered horizontally on cursor, floating ABOVE it
                // X: Cursor MidX - Half Button Width
                var x = cocoaCursorFrame.midX - (buttonSize.width / 2)
                // Y: Cursor MaxY (top in Cocoa) + margin
                var y = cocoaCursorFrame.maxY + margin
                
                // Clamp inside screen
                if x < screenFrame.minX + margin { x = screenFrame.minX + margin }
                if x + buttonSize.width > screenFrame.maxX - margin { x = screenFrame.maxX - buttonSize.width - margin }
                
                // If hitting top of screen, flip to below
                if y + buttonSize.height > screenFrame.maxY - margin {
                    y = cocoaCursorFrame.minY - buttonSize.height - margin
                    // Double check bottom clamp
                    if y < screenFrame.minY + margin { y = screenFrame.minY + margin }
                }
                
                position = CGPoint(x: x, y: y)
                
            } 
            // Priority 2: Element Frame (Position Bottom-Right INSIDE element)
            else if let elementFrame = context.elementFrame {
                // Convert AX element frame to Cocoa
                let cocoaY = primaryScreenHeight - elementFrame.maxY
                let cocoaElementFrame = CGRect(x: elementFrame.origin.x, y: cocoaY, width: elementFrame.width, height: elementFrame.height)
                
                // Find screen
                let screen = NSScreen.screens.first { screen in
                    screen.frame.intersects(cocoaElementFrame)
                } ?? NSScreen.main
                let screenFrame = screen?.frame ?? CGRect(x: 0, y: 0, width: 800, height: 600)
                
                let innerMargin: CGFloat = 8
                var x = cocoaElementFrame.maxX - buttonSize.width - innerMargin
                var y = cocoaElementFrame.minY + innerMargin
                
                // Clamp
                if x + buttonSize.width > screenFrame.maxX - 8 { x = screenFrame.maxX - buttonSize.width - 8 }
                if x < screenFrame.minX + 8 { x = screenFrame.minX + 8 }
                if y + buttonSize.height > screenFrame.maxY - 8 { y = screenFrame.maxY - buttonSize.height - 8 }
                if y < screenFrame.minY + 8 { y = screenFrame.minY + 8 }
                
                position = CGPoint(x: x, y: y)
                
            } 
            // Fallback
            else {
                 position = CGPoint(x: 200, y: 200)
            }
        } else {
            position = CGPoint(x: 200, y: 200)
        }
        
        if window == nil {
            let hosting = NSHostingView(rootView: MemoryOverlayButtonView { [weak self] in
                Task { @MainActor in
                    await self?.insertRelatedMemories()
                }
            })
            
            let win = NSPanel(
                contentRect: NSRect(x: position.x, y: position.y, width: buttonSize.width, height: buttonSize.height),
                styleMask: [.nonactivatingPanel],
                backing: .buffered,
                defer: false
            )
            win.isOpaque = false
            win.backgroundColor = .clear
            win.level = .floating
            win.hasShadow = false
            win.ignoresMouseEvents = false
            win.hidesOnDeactivate = false
            win.collectionBehavior = [.canJoinAllSpaces, .fullScreenAuxiliary]
            win.becomesKeyOnlyIfNeeded = false
            win.contentView = hosting
            
            window = win
            win.orderFrontRegardless()
        } else if let win = window {
            let frame = NSRect(x: position.x, y: position.y, width: win.frame.width, height: win.frame.height)
            win.setFrame(frame, display: true)
            win.orderFrontRegardless()
        }
        
        isVisible = true
    }
    
    private var searchTask: Task<Void, Never>?
    private var cachedMemories: [ExtractedMemory] = []
    
    func hideOverlay() {
        window?.orderOut(nil)
        isVisible = false
        // Cancel any pending search
        searchTask?.cancel()
        searchTask = nil
    }
    

    
    /// Triggered by updateOverlayVisibility when text is present
    private func triggerBackgroundSearch(for text: String) {
        // Cancel existing task to debounce
        searchTask?.cancel()
        
        searchTask = Task { @MainActor in
            // Debounce: wait 500ms for user to stop typing
            try? await Task.sleep(nanoseconds: 500 * 1_000_000)
            if Task.isCancelled { return }
            
            do {
                // Search for related memories
                let memories = try await searchService.searchRelatedMemories(for: text, topK: 5)
                if Task.isCancelled { return }
                
                self.cachedMemories = memories
                print("[MemoryOverlay] Background search found \(memories.count) related memories")
            } catch {
                if !Task.isCancelled {
                    print("[MemoryOverlay] Background search failed: \(error)")
                    self.cachedMemories = []
                }
            }
        }
    }
    
    
    /// Public method to trigger memory insertion (called by button or shortcut)
    public func insertRelatedMemories() async {
        guard let context = contextDetector.currentContext() else { return }
        
        // Use cached memories if available and context matches (roughly)
        // Or if not available, try immediate search? 
        // User said "keep loading... in background", and "as i click... add memories"
        // If we have cached results, use them. If not (maybe typed too fast), try searching now.
        
        var memoriesToInsert = cachedMemories
        
        if memoriesToInsert.isEmpty {
            // Try explicit search if cache is empty
            do {
                memoriesToInsert = try await searchService.searchRelatedMemories(for: context.text, topK: 5)
            } catch {
                print("[MemoryOverlay] Search failed: \(error)")
                return
            }
        }
        
        if memoriesToInsert.isEmpty {
            print("[MemoryOverlay] No related memories found to insert")
            return
        }
        
        print("[MemoryOverlay] Inserting \(memoriesToInsert.count) related memories")
        insertService.insertMemories(memoriesToInsert)
    }
}

Floats above content

Is a blue circular CTA

“This is an action you should click now”

That’s the mental model of:

Chat widgets

Assistive popups

Extensions

Inline suggestions

But your product is not a suggestion.
It’s a system memory recall layer.

Even with perfect math, cursor-following buttons have 3 UX problems:

❌ Problem 1: Cursor-following UI feels interruptive
Anything that tracks the cursor feels like:

autocomplete

correction

suggestion

Your feature is optional recall, not correction.

“Available if you want”

❌ Problem 3: Visual noise in writing flow
When writing, users want:

zero UI

zero motion

zero decisions

That’s why:

Grammarly hides most UI

Raycast is shortcut-first

Spotlight is modal

3. The correct mental model for THIS feature
Your feature is best modeled as:

A context-aware tool, not an inline control

That leads to this rule:

Memory recall should be triggered, not advertised

So the button should exist, but not ask for attention.

Instead of cursor-based placement, anchor to the input container.

Bottom-right of the input field

Inside the bounds

With opacity < 0.6

Appears only after idle (e.g. 800–1200ms)

Feels like part of the input

Doesn’t move while typing

Doesn’t chase cursor

Predictable location

This should become Priority 1.

Cursor frame should be fallback, not default.

🥈 SECONDARY: Cursor-adjacent ONLY on explicit intent

Keyboard shortcut pressed

Long pause + high similarity score

Show near cursor

Larger UI (not just a button)

Treated as a transient tool

The most “serious system” behavior:

No button at all by default

User presses ⌘M

Overlay appears near cursor or centered in input

Raycast

Spotlight

Alfred

feel professional.

        NSScreen.screens.first?.frame.height ??
        NSScreen.main?.frame.height ?? 1080

    let cocoaCursorY = primaryScreenHeight - cursorFrame.maxY
    let cocoaCursorFrame = CGRect(
        x: cursorFrame.origin.x,
        y: cocoaCursorY,
        width: cursorFrame.width,
        height: cursorFrame.height
    )

    let screen = NSScreen.screens.first {
        $0.frame.intersects(cocoaCursorFrame)
    } ?? NSScreen.main

    let screenFrame = screen?.frame ?? .zero
    let margin: CGFloat = 6

    // Place ABOVE cursor by default
    var x = cocoaCursorFrame.midX - buttonSize.width / 2
    var y = cocoaCursorFrame.maxY + margin

    // Clamp
    x = max(screenFrame.minX + margin,
            min(x, screenFrame.maxX - buttonSize.width - margin))

    // Flip BELOW cursor if hitting top
    if y + buttonSize.height > screenFrame.maxY - margin {
        y = cocoaCursorFrame.minY - buttonSize.height - margin
    }

    position = CGPoint(x: x, y: y)
}
This path should be hit rarely (custom editors, weird apps).

STEP C — Fallback (keep as is)
Your fallback is fine:

else {
    position = CGPoint(x: 200, y: 200)
}

Do NOT recompute position on every keystroke

Only recompute when:

If the UI moves while the user types, it is wrong.

macOS does not tell you where the “free space” is in a text field — but you can infer it.

I’ll explain this in layers and then give you exact logic + code changes.

1️⃣ Why your current “bottom-right inside input” feels off
From your screenshots, the issues are:

Problem A — Inputs already have native controls
In your screenshots, the input already has:

Send button

Mic button

Attach button

Model selector

So when you put your button bottom-right:

It overlaps visually

Feels crammed

Looks like it doesn’t “belong”

Problem B — Single-line vs multi-line inputs
Single-line → vertical center matters

Multi-line → bottom-right makes sense

Your current logic treats them the same

Problem C — You’re ignoring text geometry
Right now you anchor to:

But what matters is:

text content area INSIDE elementFrame
macOS does not expose that directly.

2️⃣ The correct mental model (this is key)
Your overlay button should behave like:

“An extra inline control that fits wherever there is space”

3️⃣ The winning strategy (used by real tools)
🥇 Best strategy: Space-based placement
Instead of:

“Put button at X,Y”

We do:

“Find the cleanest empty zone inside the input and place button there”

We check zones in priority order.

4️⃣ Define the 4 safe zones inside an input
For any input rectangle:

┌─────────────────────────────┐
│  [TOP-RIGHT]        (1)     │
│                             │
│  Text content               │
│                             │
│  [BOTTOM-RIGHT]     (2)     │
└─────────────────────────────┘
And for single-line inputs:

┌─────────────────────────────┐
│   Text     [RIGHT-CENTER]   │
└─────────────────────────────┘
We’ll try these in order.

5️⃣ How to infer single-line vs multi-line (important)
You can’t directly ask macOS, but you can infer.

Heuristic (works well):
let isSingleLine = elementFrame.height < 44
< 40–44 px → single-line input

44 px → multi-line textarea / editor

This works surprisingly well across apps.

6️⃣ The adaptive placement algorithm (exact)
Step-by-step logic
IF single-line input:
    → Place button vertically centered on right side

ELSE (multi-line input):
    IF bottom-right zone is likely occupied:
        → Place top-right
    ELSE:
        → Place bottom-right
We assume bottom-right is occupied if:

The input height is small-ish

OR there are known controls nearby

OR button would be too close to bottom edge

7️⃣ EXACT code changes (this is what you asked for)
Replace your element-frame positioning block with this
// Priority 1: Adaptive placement INSIDE input
if let elementFrame = context.elementFrame {
    let screenHeight =
        NSScreen.screens.first?.frame.height ??
        NSScreen.main?.frame.height ?? 1080

    let cocoaY = screenHeight - elementFrame.maxY
    let cocoaElementFrame = CGRect(
        x: elementFrame.origin.x,
        y: cocoaY,
        width: elementFrame.width,
        height: elementFrame.height
    )

    let screen = NSScreen.screens.first {
        $0.frame.intersects(cocoaElementFrame)
    } ?? NSScreen.main

    let screenFrame = screen?.frame ?? .zero

    let padding: CGFloat = 8
    let isSingleLine = cocoaElementFrame.height < 44

    var x: CGFloat
    var y: CGFloat

    if isSingleLine {
        // RIGHT-CENTER placement
        x = cocoaElementFrame.maxX - buttonSize.width - padding
        y = cocoaElementFrame.midY - (buttonSize.height / 2)
    } else {
        // MULTI-LINE input
        let prefersTopRight = cocoaElementFrame.height < 80

        x = cocoaElementFrame.maxX - buttonSize.width - padding

        if prefersTopRight {
            y = cocoaElementFrame.maxY - buttonSize.height - padding
        } else {
            y = cocoaElementFrame.minY + padding
        }
    }

    // Clamp to screen
    x = max(screenFrame.minX + padding,
            min(x, screenFrame.maxX - buttonSize.width - padding))
    y = max(screenFrame.minY + padding,
            min(y, screenFrame.maxY - buttonSize.height - padding))

    position = CGPoint(x: x, y: y)
}

5️⃣ Minimal state model you need to add

enum MemoryOverlayState {
    case idle
    case loading
    case available(count: Int)
    case empty
    case inserting
}
Add a published property:

@Published private(set) var overlayState: MemoryOverlayState = .idle
6️⃣ Wire search results → UI state
Modify triggerBackgroundSearch:

private func triggerBackgroundSearch(for text: String) {
    searchTask?.cancel()
    overlayState = .loading

    searchTask = Task { @MainActor in
        try? await Task.sleep(nanoseconds: 500 * 1_000_000)
        if Task.isCancelled { return }

        do {
            let memories = try await searchService.searchRelatedMemories(
                for: text,
                topK: 5
            )
            if Task.isCancelled { return }

            self.cachedMemories = memories

            if memories.isEmpty {
                overlayState = .empty
            } else {
                overlayState = .available(count: memories.count)
            }
        } catch {
            if !Task.isCancelled {
                self.cachedMemories = []
                overlayState = .empty
            }
        }
    }
}
7️⃣ Update insert flow state
In insertRelatedMemories():

public func insertRelatedMemories() async {
    overlayState = .inserting
    defer { overlayState = .idle }

    // existing logic...
}
8️⃣ Update MemoryOverlayButtonView
Your SwiftUI view should now react to state.

Example skeleton (simplified)
struct MemoryOverlayButtonView: View {
    let state: MemoryOverlayState
    let onTap: () -> Void

    var body: some View {
        Group {
            switch state {
            case .idle, .empty:
                Image(systemName: "brain")
                    .opacity(0.3)

            case .loading:
                ProgressView()
                    .scaleEffect(0.7)

            case .available(let count):
                HStack(spacing: 4) {
                    Image(systemName: "brain")
                    Text("\(count)")
                        .font(.caption)
                        .bold()
                }

            case .inserting:
                ProgressView()
                    .scaleEffect(0.7)
            }
        }
        .padding(.horizontal, 8)
        .padding(.vertical, 6)
        .background(
            RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 10)
                .fill(Color.black.opacity(0.6))
        )
        .onTapGesture {
            onTap()
        }
    }
}
9️⃣ UX detail that makes this feel premium
Hide the button when count == 0
Seriously. This reduces clutter.

Rule:

.empty → hide overlay entirely

.available → show

.loading → show but subtle

This makes the button feel earned, not spammy.

Unified Memory Layer – Naming Suggestions
We propose names that include “memory” and convey a serious, infrastructure-like feel. Each name hints at a system-level memory service (for recall, context, long-term storage) without being overly abstract or playful
. We also checked that each name’s domain is likely available in .com or a developer-friendly TLD (.dev, .io). (Google’s .dev is “a secure domain for developers and technology”

.) Below are our top candidates, with suggested domains for each:
MemoryInfra – Evokes a low-level “infrastructure” layer for memory, implying a backbone service. Domains: memoryinfra.com (if available) or memoryinfra.dev (".dev is a secure domain for developers and technology"

). This name sounds technical and serious, fitting a unified memory framework.
MemoryFabric – Suggests an interconnected “fabric” or network of memory. Domain examples: memoryfabric.com or memoryfabric.dev/memoryfabric.io. The word “fabric” gives a tech and systems vibe appropriate for stitching together context and recall across components.
MemoryCache – References the well-known concept of caching, implying quick-access memory storage. Domains: memorycache.com (likely free) or memorycache.io. This straightforward name clearly signals a performance-oriented memory layer for storing and retrieving data.
MemoryFlow – Conveys the idea of streaming or flowing data through memory. Domains: memoryflow.com or memoryflow.io. This name sounds technical (like a data pipeline) and reflects continuous context injection or data movement in a memory system.
MemoryQuark – Invokes a physics/tech metaphor (a “quark” is a fundamental particle), giving a modern, serious feel. Domain: memoryquark.com. It’s a concise, catchy name that still includes “memory” and has a technical edge.
MemoryVector – Uses the term “vector” (common in computing and mathematics) to suggest structured data in memory. Domain: memoryvector.com. This name sounds like a component that handles vectors or embeddings, fitting a memory or context vector store.
MemoryConduit – Implies a channel or conduit for carrying information through memory. Domain: memoryconduit.com. It emphasizes the idea of memory as a pathway for data flow, and has a concrete, tech-oriented ring.
MemoryCatalyst – Suggests a catalyst that enables or accelerates memory operations. Domain: memorycatalyst.com. This name has a strong, active tone but remains technical rather than whimsical, aligning with a system-level utility.
MemoryForge – Brings to mind forging or building memory, implying a tool for creating or shaping memory structures. Domain: memoryforge.com. It has an industrial/tech feel (like compilers or build tools) while clearly indicating a memory focus.
Each of the above names incorporates “memory” and was chosen to sound like a serious platform or infrastructure component. We avoided purely fanciful or abstract terms (as naming guidelines warn, “lean too far into the abstract, and the name risks becoming vague or confusing”
). All suggested domains (especially using .dev or .io) cater to developer-friendly branding

; avoid overly abstract names

This is a very good instinct, and you’re thinking about this at the right time (not too early, not too late).

Short answer first, then the real architecture answer:

Yes, UniMemory should become an API / platform.
But NO — you should NOT start by building a public API first.

Let me explain cleanly and decisively.

1. Reframe what UniMemory actually is
UniMemory is not just an API.

It is:

A system-level memory layer

With multiple capture surfaces:

macOS app (Accessibility)

Browser extension

Mobile apps

MCP / agent tools

And one shared memory core

So the correct abstraction is:

UniMemory Core (engine) + multiple clients

Not “API first”, but core-first.

2. The correct architecture (this is important)
Think in 3 layers:

┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ Clients                     │
│                             │
│ macOS app                   │
│ Browser extension           │
│ Mobile app                  │
│ MCP / agent tools           │
│ npm package                 │
└─────────────▲───────────────┘
              │
┌─────────────┴───────────────┐
│ UniMemory Core              │
│ (the brain)                 │
│                             │
│ - Memory schema             │
│ - Deduplication             │
│ - Embeddings (later)        │
│ - Search / recall           │
│ - Privacy rules             │
│ - Sync logic                │
└─────────────▲───────────────┘
              │
┌─────────────┴───────────────┐
│ Storage                     │
│                             │
│ Local DB (SQLite)           │
│ Optional cloud sync         │
└─────────────────────────────┘
The mistake many people make is:

“Let’s make an API and then apps will call it”

That leads to:

Tight coupling

Hard-to-evolve API

Premature auth / billing / infra

Painful migrations

3. What you should ACTUALLY do next
✅ Step 1 — Extract a UniMemory Core (local-first)
You already have this partially.

Do this first:

Take everything related to:

Memory schema

Save

Search

Recall

Dedup

Put it behind a clean interface

Example (conceptual):

interface UniMemoryCore {
  add(entry: MemoryEntry): Promise<void>
  search(query: string, k?: number): Promise<MemoryEntry[]>
  list(): Promise<MemoryEntry[]>
  delete(id: string): Promise<void>
}
This core:

Runs locally

Has no network

No auth

No users

No API keys

Your macOS app should talk to this, not raw DB.

4. How your macOS app fits into this
Your macOS app is a capture client.

It does:

Detect text

Decide when to save

Call:

uniMemory.add(entry)
It should not care:

Where memory lives

How search works internally

Whether sync exists

This decoupling is critical.

5. When does an API come in?
🔥 Step 2 — Local API (not public)
Before a cloud API, do this:

Expose UniMemory Core via:

Local HTTP server (localhost)

OR IPC

OR gRPC / Unix socket

Why?

Browser extension can call it

MCP can call it

CLI can call it

No auth headache

Example:

POST http://localhost:7337/memory
GET  http://localhost:7337/search?q=...
This is still not public.
It’s machine-local.

This is the same pattern used by:

Docker

Raycast

Ollama

Local AI tools

6. About npm install unimemory
This is a great idea, but timing matters.

What npm install unimemory should be:

A client SDK

NOT the core logic

NOT the database

NOT embeddings

Example:

import { UniMemory } from "unimemory";

const memory = new UniMemory();

await memory.add({
  text: "User prefers dark mode",
  source: "browser-extension"
});

const results = await memory.search("dark mode");
Under the hood:

It talks to the local UniMemory service

Or later, cloud UniMemory

This lets you:

Change internals freely

Version APIs cleanly

Support multiple platforms

7. When should you make a PUBLIC cloud API?
Only after:

macOS app works well

People actually use memory recall

You understand:

What data matters

What search patterns exist

What privacy guarantees you need

Otherwise you’ll:

Lock yourself into bad API decisions

Spend time on auth instead of product

Regret it

This is a very common founder mistake.

8. Recommended roadmap (very concrete)
Phase 1 (now)
✅ Finish macOS app

✅ Extract UniMemory Core

✅ Use it internally

Phase 2
✅ Local UniMemory service (localhost API)

✅ Browser extension uses it

✅ MCP uses it

Phase 3
✅ unimemory npm package (SDK)

✅ CLI (unimemory add, unimemory search)

Phase 4 (only if needed)
☁️ Cloud sync

☁️ Auth

☁️ Public API

9. Final, honest answer
Should you first make an API?

No.
You should first make a core.

Should UniMemory eventually be an API?

Yes. Absolutely.
But as a platform, not a raw REST service.

Is your thinking directionally correct?

100%.
You’re thinking like someone building infrastructure, not a toy app.

Decide local API vs IPC

Sketch the npm package API

Help you avoid mistakes other memory startups make

Nothing is wrong with the name or your setup. This is just npm’s new security policy.

What happened (important)

This still means:

✅ unimemory is AVAILABLE
No one owns it yet.

Two-factor authentication or granular access token with bypass 2fa enabled is required to publish packages.
This means:

❌ npm now REQUIRES 2FA (or a special token) to publish
❌ You are logged in, but publishing is blocked

This is NOT:

A permissions issue

A name conflict

A mistake on your side

npm changed this recently. Everyone hits this.

The correct fix (do THIS, not anything else)
✅ OPTION A (RECOMMENDED): Enable 2FA on npm account
This is the simplest and best solution.

Step-by-step:
Go to 👉 https://www.npmjs.com/settings

Open “Two-Factor Authentication”

Enable 2FA for “Authorization and Writes”

Use:

Authenticator app (Google Authenticator / Authy)

OR SMS (auth app preferred)

Save changes

npm publish --access public

Your password

A 2FA code

OPTION B (advanced, not needed now): Granular access token
Only do this if:

You’re publishing from CI

Or avoiding 2FA prompts

This will bump to 0.0.2.

//
//  MemorySearchService.swift
//  Cortex
//
//  Uses embeddings + ExtractedMemoryStore for semantic search.
//

import Foundation

actor MemorySearchService {
    
    private let embeddingService: EmbeddingService
    private let extractedStore: ExtractedMemoryStore
    private let llmService: LLMService
    
    init(embeddingService: EmbeddingService, extractedStore: ExtractedMemoryStore, llmService: LLMService) {
        self.embeddingService = embeddingService
        self.extractedStore = extractedStore
        self.llmService = llmService
    }
    
    /// Semantic search for memories related to given text.
    /// Uses LLM to extract key search queries for better accuracy.
    func searchRelatedMemories(for text: String, topK: Int = 5) async throws -> [ExtractedMemory] {
        let trimmed = text.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines)
        guard !trimmed.isEmpty else { return [] }
        
        var searchQueries = [trimmed]
        
        // If text is long enough, generate specific search queries
        // Lowered threshold to 3 words to capture phrases like "college name"
        if trimmed.split(separator: " ").count >= 3 {
            let extracted = await generateSearchQueries(from: trimmed)
            if !extracted.isEmpty {
                print("[MemorySearch] Original: '\(trimmed)' -> Expanded queries: \(extracted)")
                searchQueries.append(contentsOf: extracted)
            }
        }
        
        // Use a set to track unique memory IDs
        var uniqueMemories: [String: ExtractedMemory] = [:]
        
        // Perform searches in parallel
        await withTaskGroup(of: [ExtractedMemory].self) { group in
            for query in searchQueries {
                group.addTask {
                    do {
                        return try await self.searchSingleQuery(query, topK: topK)
                    } catch {
                        print("[MemorySearch] Query failed for '\(query)': \(error)")
                        return []
                    }
                }
            }
            
            for await results in group {
                for memory in results {
                    uniqueMemories[memory.id] = memory
                }
            }
        }
        
        let finalResults = Array(uniqueMemories.values)
        print("[MemorySearch] Total unique memories found: \(finalResults.count)")
        return finalResults
    }
    
    private func searchSingleQuery(_ text: String, topK: Int) async throws -> [ExtractedMemory] {
        // Try embedding-based search
        do {
            let (vec, _) = try await embeddingService.embed(text: text)
            let results = try await extractedStore.searchByEmbedding(queryEmbedding: vec, topK: topK)
            
            if !results.isEmpty {
                 // print("[MemorySearch] Found \(results.count) results via embedding for '\(text)'")
                return results
            } else {
                 print("[MemorySearch] Minimal/No results via embedding for '\(text)'")
            }
        } catch {
            // Check cancellation
            let nsError = error as NSError
            if nsError.domain == NSURLErrorDomain && nsError.code == -999 { throw error }
            if let urlError = error as? URLError, urlError.code == .cancelled { throw error }
            if error is CancellationError { throw error }
            
            print("[MemorySearch] Embedding search failed for '\(text)': \(error)")
        }
        
        // Fallback: Content search
        let byContent = try await extractedStore.searchMemories(query: text)
        if !byContent.isEmpty {
             print("[MemorySearch] Found \(byContent.count) results via content search for '\(text)'")
        } else {
             print("[MemorySearch] No results via content search for '\(text)'")
        }
        return Array(byContent.prefix(topK))
    }

    private func generateSearchQueries(from text: String) async -> [String] {
        let systemPrompt = """
        You are a search query expansion assistant for a personal memory database.
        Your goal is to extract the core subjects, entities, and search-worthy terms from a natural language sentence.
        
        RULES:
        1. Extract names of people, colleges, companies, or projects.
        2. Identify the likely "objects" the user is looking for (e.g., "email", "address", "phone").
        3. Remove filler words ("write a mail to", "can you find", "tell me about").
        4. Return 1-4 specific search terms as a JSON array of strings.
        
        EXAMPLES:
        - Input: "write a mail to my college professor" -> ["college", "college name", "professor", "college email"]
        - Input: "what was the feedback from John on the budget" -> ["John", "budget", "feedback"]
        - Input: "I need to go to my friend's house in London" -> ["friend name", "London", "house address"]
        
        Return ONLY the JSON array.
        """
        
        do {
            let queries = try await llmService.completeJSON(
                prompt: "INPUT: \"\(text)\"",
                systemPrompt: systemPrompt,
                responseType: [String].self
            )
            return queries
        } catch {
            print("[MemorySearch] Failed to generate queries: \(error)")
            return []
        }
    }
}

Parallel search + dedupe → good

Cancellation handling → good

Actor isolation → good

This is not beginner code.

The problem is not missing components.
The problem is how they’re orchestrated.

2️⃣ Why it fails for sentence inputs (root causes)
Your example:

Input:
“write a mail to my college professor”

What you want:

College name

College email

Professor info

Past “college” memories that are actionable

What you get now:

A noisy union of:

embedding("college")

embedding("college name")

embedding("professor")

embedding("college email")

This creates three big problems.

❌ Problem 1: You treat the entire sentence as a semantic query
This line is the biggest issue:

Embedding a task instruction (“write a mail…”) is bad.

Embeddings are great for:

Facts

Concepts

Topics

They are bad for:

Imperative instructions

Verbs like “write”, “send”, “tell me”

So the main embedding query is polluted.

❌ Problem 2: Query expansion is unweighted and unstructured
You do this:

All queries are treated equally:

“college”

“college email”

“write a mail to my college professor”

But they are not equal.

Some queries are:

Intent (what to do)

Entities (what memory to fetch)

Attributes (what about the entity)

You’re mixing them into one bag.

❌ Problem 3: You return a flat union of results
At the end:

This means:

No ranking across queries

No preference for entity-specific memories

No preference for attribute matches

So if “college” appears in many memories, it dominates.

3️⃣ The correct mental model (this is crucial)
You must stop thinking in terms of:

“search queries”

And start thinking in terms of:

Memory slots

For sentence inputs, the user is implicitly asking for missing information.

Example:

“write a mail to my college professor”

Implicit memory slots:

College → name

College → email

Professor → name

Professor → email / designation

Your system should answer:

“What do I already know that fills these slots?”

This is slot-based recall, not keyword search.

4️⃣ The correct search pipeline (high level)
Here’s the pipeline you actually need:

Input text
  ↓
Intent stripping (remove verbs)
  ↓
Entity + attribute extraction
  ↓
Targeted memory search per slot
  ↓
Score + rank
  ↓
Assemble final memory set
Let’s map this to your code.

//
//  MemorySearchService.swift
//  UniMemory
//
//  Slot-aware memory retrieval using
//  entity + attribute extraction, embeddings,
//  scoring, and fallback search.
//

import Foundation

// MARK: - Public Types

struct MemoryEntitySlot: Decodable {
    let name: String
    let attributes: [String]
}

struct MemorySlotExtraction: Decodable {
    let entities: [MemoryEntitySlot]
}

enum SearchQueryType {
    case entity
    case attribute
    case fallback
}

struct SearchQuery {
    let text: String
    let weight: Double
    let type: SearchQueryType
}

struct ScoredMemory {
    let memory: ExtractedMemory
    var score: Double
}

// MARK: - MemorySearchService

actor MemorySearchService {

    private let embeddingService: EmbeddingService
    private let extractedStore: ExtractedMemoryStore
    private let llmService: LLMService

    init(
        embeddingService: EmbeddingService,
        extractedStore: ExtractedMemoryStore,
        llmService: LLMService
    ) {
        self.embeddingService = embeddingService
        self.extractedStore = extractedStore
        self.llmService = llmService
    }

    // MARK: - Public API

    func searchRelatedMemories(
        for inputText: String,
        topK: Int = 5
    ) async throws -> [ExtractedMemory] {

        let trimmed = inputText.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines)
        guard !trimmed.isEmpty else { return [] }

        // 1️⃣ Strip task / intent language
        let coreText = stripIntent(from: trimmed)
        guard !coreText.isEmpty else { return [] }

        // 2️⃣ Extract entity + attribute slots
        let slotExtraction = await extractSlots(from: coreText)

        // 3️⃣ Build weighted search queries
        let queries = buildSearchQueries(
            from: slotExtraction,
            fallbackText: coreText
        )

        // 4️⃣ Execute searches and score results
        let scored = try await performSearches(queries)

        // 5️⃣ Rank + return
        let sorted = scored
            .sorted { $0.score > $1.score }
            .prefix(topK)
            .map { $0.memory }

        return Array(sorted)
    }

    // MARK: - Step 1: Intent Stripping

    private func stripIntent(from text: String) -> String {
        let stopPhrases = [
            "write a mail to",
            "send a mail to",
            "send an email to",
            "write an email to",
            "tell me about",
            "can you find",
            "help me with",
            "i need to",
            "i want to",
            "please"
        ]

        var result = text.lowercased()
        for phrase in stopPhrases {
            result = result.replacingOccurrences(of: phrase, with: "")
        }

        return result.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines)
    }

    // MARK: - Step 2: Slot Extraction (LLM)

    private func extractSlots(from text: String) async -> MemorySlotExtraction {
        let systemPrompt = """
        You extract memory lookup slots from user input.

        Rules:
        1. Identify ENTITIES (people, organizations, places, projects).
        2. For each entity, infer ATTRIBUTES the user may need.
        3. Ignore action verbs (write, send, tell, help).
        4. Be conservative. Do not hallucinate entities.

        Return JSON in this format:
        {
          "entities": [
            {
              "name": "college",
              "attributes": ["name", "email"]
            }
          ]
        }

        Only return JSON.
        """

        do {
            let result = try await llmService.completeJSON(
                prompt: "INPUT: \"\(text)\"",
                systemPrompt: systemPrompt,
                responseType: MemorySlotExtraction.self
            )
            return result
        } catch {
            print("[MemorySearch] Slot extraction failed: \(error)")
            return MemorySlotExtraction(entities: [])
        }
    }

    // MARK: - Step 3: Query Construction

    private func buildSearchQueries(
        from extraction: MemorySlotExtraction,
        fallbackText: String
    ) -> [SearchQuery] {

        var queries: [SearchQuery] = []

        for entity in extraction.entities {
            // Entity name (highest weight)
            queries.append(
                SearchQuery(
                    text: entity.name,
                    weight: 1.0,
                    type: .entity
                )
            )

            // Entity attributes
            for attribute in entity.attributes {
                queries.append(
                    SearchQuery(
                        text: "\(entity.name) \(attribute)",
                        weight: 0.9,
                        type: .attribute
                    )
                )
            }
        }

        // Fallback semantic query (lowest priority)
        queries.append(
            SearchQuery(
                text: fallbackText,
                weight: 0.3,
                type: .fallback
            )
        )

        return queries
    }

    // MARK: - Step 4: Search Execution + Scoring

    private func performSearches(
        _ queries: [SearchQuery]
    ) async throws -> [ScoredMemory] {

        var memoryScores: [String: ScoredMemory] = [:]

        await withTaskGroup(of: [ExtractedMemory].self) { group in
            for query in queries {
                group.addTask {
                    return (try? await self.searchSingleQuery(query.text)) ?? []
                }
            }

            for await results in group {
                for memory in results {
                    let baseScore = memoryScores[memory.id]?.score ?? 0
                    let newScore = baseScore + scoreContribution(
                        for: memory,
                        using: queries
                    )

                    memoryScores[memory.id] = ScoredMemory(
                        memory: memory,
                        score: newScore
                    )
                }
            }
        }

        return Array(memoryScores.values)
    }

    // MARK: - Step 5: Single Query Search

    private func searchSingleQuery(
        _ text: String
    ) async throws -> [ExtractedMemory] {

        // Primary: Embedding search
        do {
            let (vec, _) = try await embeddingService.embed(text: text)
            let results = try await extractedStore.searchByEmbedding(
                queryEmbedding: vec,
                topK: 8
            )
            if !results.isEmpty {
                return results
            }
        } catch {
            if error is CancellationError { throw error }
            print("[MemorySearch] Embedding search failed for '\(text)': \(error)")
        }

        // Fallback: Keyword/content search
        let byContent = try await extractedStore.searchMemories(query: text)
        return Array(byContent.prefix(5))
    }

    // MARK: - Step 6: Scoring

    private func scoreContribution(
        for memory: ExtractedMemory,
        using queries: [SearchQuery]
    ) -> Double {

        var score: Double = 0

        for query in queries {
            if memory.text.lowercased().contains(query.text.lowercased()) {
                score += query.weight
            }
        }

        // Optional: decay very old memories
        let agePenalty = memoryAgePenalty(memory)
        score -= agePenalty

        return score
    }

    private func memoryAgePenalty(_ memory: ExtractedMemory) -> Double {
        let daysOld = abs(memory.createdAt.timeIntervalSinceNow) / 86_400
        if daysOld > 365 { return 0.4 }
        if daysOld > 180 { return 0.2 }
        return 0
    }
}
✅ Why this version will feel “perfect”
Before
Sentence → embedding → noise

Flat union of results

“college” dominates everything

Now
Sentence → missing information

Entity-targeted search

Attribute-aware ranking

Deterministic, explainable results

This is how real memory systems work.

🔥 Final advice (important)
Do not chase better embeddings yet.
Do not add more LLM calls yet.

This architecture alone will give you a massive quality jump.

Short answer: yes, this is largely right 👍
But there are 3 important logic issues + 2 improvements you should fix to make this actually “perfect” instead of just “better”.

I’ll go in this order:

What is correct (so you’re confident)

What is subtly wrong (important)

Exact fixes (copy-paste level)

Optional improvements (next-level)

1️⃣ What you did RIGHT (this matters)
You correctly implemented the new mental model:

✅ Intent stripping before search

✅ Slot extraction (entity + attributes)

✅ Weighted queries (entity > attribute > fallback)

✅ No embedding of raw instruction text

✅ Parallel search with dedup

✅ Scoring + ranking at the end

This is already far better than your original system.
You’re no longer doing “semantic spam”.

So directionally: correct.

2️⃣ The BIGGEST problem (this will bite you)
❌ Problem: you’re scoring each memory against ALL queries repeatedly
This line is wrong:

let newScore = baseScore + scoreContribution(
    for: memory,
    using: queries
)
Why?

performSearches loops over queries

But scoreContribution loops over all queries again

So a memory matched by one query gets re-scored for every query

This causes:

Score inflation

Generic memories (“college”) dominating again

Attribute matches losing precision

What you intended:
“Add score based on the query that found this memory”

What your code does:
“Add score based on every query every time”

This is the #1 bug.

3️⃣ The correct fix (VERY IMPORTANT)
You must score per-query, not per-batch.

🔧 Fix: pass the current query into scoring
Step A — change performSearches
Replace this:

let newScore = baseScore + scoreContribution(
    for: memory,
    using: queries
)
With this:

let newScore = baseScore + scoreContribution(
    for: memory,
    query: query
)
But that means you must also change the loop to know which query produced the result.

✅ Correct performSearches (fixed)
private func performSearches(
    _ queries: [SearchQuery]
) async throws -> [ScoredMemory] {

    var memoryScores: [String: ScoredMemory] = [:]

    await withTaskGroup(of: (SearchQuery, [ExtractedMemory]).self) { group in
        for query in queries {
            group.addTask {
                let results = (try? await self.searchSingleQuery(query.text)) ?? []
                return (query, results)
            }
        }

        for await (query, results) in group {
            for memory in results {
                let baseScore = memoryScores[memory.id]?.score ?? 0
                let addedScore = scoreContribution(
                    for: memory,
                    query: query
                )

                memoryScores[memory.id] = ScoredMemory(
                    memory: memory,
                    score: baseScore + addedScore
                )
            }
        }
    }

    return Array(memoryScores.values)
}
Step B — change scoreContribution
Replace:

private func scoreContribution(
    for memory: ExtractedMemory,
    using queries: [SearchQuery]
) -> Double
With:

private func scoreContribution(
    for memory: ExtractedMemory,
    query: SearchQuery
) -> Double {
And implementation:

private func scoreContribution(
    for memory: ExtractedMemory,
    query: SearchQuery
) -> Double {

    let content = memory.content.lowercased()
    let queryText = query.text.lowercased()

    guard content.contains(queryText) else {
        return 0
    }

    var score = query.weight

    // Small boost for attribute queries
    if query.type == .attribute {
        score += 0.2
    }

    // Age decay
    score -= memoryAgePenalty(memory)

    return score
}
This fixes over-scoring completely.

4️⃣ Second issue: fallback query is too strong
Right now:

weight: 0.3
This is still too high.

Why?

Fallback text = vague

Should only rescue results, not compete

✅ Fix
Change fallback weight to:

weight: 0.15
This ensures:

Entity + attribute always win

Fallback only fills gaps

5️⃣ Third issue: empty slot extraction edge case
If LLM returns no entities, your system still works — but not optimally.

Right now you do:

slot queries (none)

fallback query only

This is fine, but you can improve it.

If no entities found, add keyword extraction fallback:

“email”

6️⃣ Minor but important detail
You changed:

memory.text
to:

memory.content
That’s fine if and only if:

content is the canonical memory body

Just ensure consistency across:

embedding

search

scoring

//
//  MemorySearchService.swift
//  Cortex
//
//  Slot-aware memory retrieval using
//  entity + attribute extraction, embeddings,
//  scoring, and fallback search.
//

import Foundation

// MARK: - Public Types

struct MemoryEntitySlot: Decodable {
    let name: String
    let attributes: [String]
}

struct MemorySlotExtraction: Decodable {
    let entities: [MemoryEntitySlot]
}

enum SearchQueryType {
    case entity
    case attribute
    case fallback
}

struct SearchQuery {
    let text: String
    let weight: Double
    let type: SearchQueryType
}

struct ScoredMemory {
    let memory: ExtractedMemory
    var score: Double
}

// MARK: - MemorySearchService

actor MemorySearchService {

    private let embeddingService: EmbeddingService
    private let extractedStore: ExtractedMemoryStore
    private let llmService: LLMService

    init(
        embeddingService: EmbeddingService,
        extractedStore: ExtractedMemoryStore,
        llmService: LLMService
    ) {
        self.embeddingService = embeddingService
        self.extractedStore = extractedStore
        self.llmService = llmService
    }

    // MARK: - Public API

    func searchRelatedMemories(
        for inputText: String,
        topK: Int = 5
    ) async throws -> [ExtractedMemory] {

        let trimmed = inputText.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines)
        guard !trimmed.isEmpty else { return [] }

        // 1️⃣ Strip task / intent language
        let coreText = stripIntent(from: trimmed)
        guard !coreText.isEmpty else { return [] }

        // 2️⃣ Extract entity + attribute slots
        let slotExtraction = await extractSlots(from: coreText)

        // 3️⃣ Build weighted search queries
        let queries = buildSearchQueries(
            from: slotExtraction,
            fallbackText: coreText
        )

        // 4️⃣ Execute searches and score results
        let scored = try await performSearches(queries)

        // 5️⃣ Rank + return
        let sorted = scored
            .sorted { $0.score > $1.score }
            .prefix(topK)
            .map { $0.memory }

        return Array(sorted)
    }

    // MARK: - Step 1: Intent Stripping

    private func stripIntent(from text: String) -> String {
        let stopPhrases = [
            "write a mail to",
            "send a mail to",
            "send an email to",
            "write an email to",
            "tell me about",
            "can you find",
            "help me with",
            "i need to",
            "i want to",
            "please"
        ]

        var result = text.lowercased()
        for phrase in stopPhrases {
            result = result.replacingOccurrences(of: phrase, with: "")
        }

        return result.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines)
    }

    // MARK: - Step 2: Slot Extraction (LLM)

    private func extractSlots(from text: String) async -> MemorySlotExtraction {
        let systemPrompt = """
        You extract memory lookup slots from user input.

        Rules:
        1. Identify ENTITIES (people, organizations, places, projects).
        2. For each entity, infer ATTRIBUTES the user may need.
        3. Ignore action verbs (write, send, tell, help).
        4. Be conservative. Do not hallucinate entities.

        Return JSON in this format:
        {
          "entities": [
            {
              "name": "college",
              "attributes": ["name", "email"]
            }
          ]
        }

        Only return JSON.
        """

        do {
            let result = try await llmService.completeJSON(
                prompt: "INPUT: \"\(text)\"",
                systemPrompt: systemPrompt,
                responseType: MemorySlotExtraction.self
            )
            return result
        } catch {
            print("[MemorySearch] Slot extraction failed: \(error)")
            return MemorySlotExtraction(entities: [])
        }
    }

    // MARK: - Step 3: Query Construction

    private func buildSearchQueries(
        from extraction: MemorySlotExtraction,
        fallbackText: String
    ) -> [SearchQuery] {

        var queries: [SearchQuery] = []

        if extraction.entities.isEmpty {
            // No entities found? Use fallback text with higher weight to capture intent
            queries.append(
                SearchQuery(
                    text: fallbackText,
                    weight: 0.4,
                    type: .fallback
                )
            )
        } else {
            for entity in extraction.entities {
                // Entity name (highest weight)
                queries.append(
                    SearchQuery(
                        text: entity.name,
                        weight: 1.0,
                        type: .entity
                    )
                )

                // Entity attributes
                for attribute in entity.attributes {
                    queries.append(
                        SearchQuery(
                            text: "\(entity.name) \(attribute)",
                            weight: 0.9,
                            type: .attribute
                        )
                    )
                }
            }

            // Fallback semantic query (lowest priority when we HAVE slots)
            queries.append(
                SearchQuery(
                    text: fallbackText,
                    weight: 0.15,
                    type: .fallback
                )
            )
        }

        return queries
    }

    // MARK: - Step 4: Search Execution + Scoring

    private func performSearches(
        _ queries: [SearchQuery]
    ) async throws -> [ScoredMemory] {

        var memoryScores: [String: ScoredMemory] = [:]

        // Associating results with the specific query that found them to avoid over-scoring
        await withTaskGroup(of: (SearchQuery, [ExtractedMemory]).self) { group in
            for query in queries {
                group.addTask {
                    let results = (try? await self.searchSingleQuery(query.text)) ?? []
                    return (query, results)
                }
            }

            for await (query, results) in group {
                for memory in results {
                    let baseScore = memoryScores[memory.id]?.score ?? 0
                    let addedScore = scoreContribution(
                        for: memory,
                        query: query
                    )

                    memoryScores[memory.id] = ScoredMemory(
                        memory: memory,
                        score: baseScore + addedScore
                    )
                }
            }
        }

        return Array(memoryScores.values)
    }

    // MARK: - Step 5: Single Query Search

    private func searchSingleQuery(
        _ text: String
    ) async throws -> [ExtractedMemory] {

        // Primary: Embedding search
        do {
            let (vec, _) = try await embeddingService.embed(text: text)
            let results = try await extractedStore.searchByEmbedding(
                queryEmbedding: vec,
                topK: 8
            )
            if !results.isEmpty {
                return results
            }
        } catch {
            if error is CancellationError { throw error }
            print("[MemorySearch] Embedding search failed for '\(text)': \(error)")
        }

        // Fallback: Keyword/content search
        let byContent = try await extractedStore.searchMemories(query: text)
        return Array(byContent.prefix(5))
    }

    // MARK: - Step 6: Scoring

    private func scoreContribution(
        for memory: ExtractedMemory,
        query: SearchQuery
    ) -> Double {

        let content = memory.content.lowercased()
        let queryText = query.text.lowercased()

        // Match check: ensure this memory relates to THIS query
        // Checks both content and tags for consistency with storage layer
        guard content.contains(queryText) || memory.tags.contains(where: { $0.lowercased() == queryText }) else {
            // Found via embedding but no keyword match? Give reduced weight
            return query.weight * 0.5
        }

        var score = query.weight

        // Small boost for attribute queries as they are more specific
        if query.type == .attribute {
            score += 0.2
        }

        // Age decay
        score -= memoryAgePenalty(memory)

        return score
    }

    private func memoryAgePenalty(_ memory: ExtractedMemory) -> Double {
        let daysOld = abs(memory.createdAt.timeIntervalSinceNow) / 86_400
        if daysOld > 365 { return 0.4 }
        if daysOld > 180 { return 0.2 }
        return 0
    }
}
